These definitions, although similar, vary both by country and across leading institutions such as the Commercial Aviation Alternative Fuels Initiative and the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). In general, for a fuel to be considered SAF it should function chemically as a Jet A blendstock while also providing a reduction in carbon intensity relative to the estimated 89-gCO e/MJ 2 baseline of fossil-based jet (ICAO 2025a). Further, SAF should utilize some form of non-fossil renewable feedstock(s). Commonly cited feedstocks for SAF include biomass, carbonaceous wastes, or various forms of fats, oils, and greases. Additionally, in an emerging field known as PtL, renewable electricity and carbon dioxide (CO ) are also being pursued as feedstocks for 2 producing SAF and SAF precursors. For the purposes of this document, we utilize a broad and inclusive definition provided by the U.S. Department of Transportation where SAF is described as any “drop-in liquid hydrocarbon jet fuel produced from renewable or waste resources that is compatible with existing aircraft and engines” (Rosales Calderon et al. 2024a). 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. To function as a drop-in fuel, SAF must meet strict requirements around performance and operability to ensure compatibility with conventional jet fuel. The chemical makeup of jet fuel (and thus of finished blends SAF with Jet A), as shown in Figure 3, broadly comprises of four hydrocarbon classes: n-alkanes, iso-alkanes, aromatics, and cycloalkanes. Each molecule class plays a critical role in meeting performance or operability needs such as energy density, thermal stability, derived cetane number, viscosity, density, and freezing point.
